To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mitochondrial DAMPs, such as mtDNA, are released in the peripheral blood during HIV infection, and this release could explain some of the inflammation present in these patients.

(i) mtDNA is present in the blood of subjects infected with HIV; (ii) mtDNA is a proinflammatory molecule; (iii) HIV infection is characterized by a proinflammatory condition; and (iv) mtDNA is able to induce a proinflammatory response during HIV infection.
mitochondrial damage is a key factor in the development of inflammation during HIV infection, and thus could be a novel target for the development of new therapeutic strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the role of mitochondria during HIV infection, in particular the role of the mitochondria in the pathogenesis of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND), and the possible therapeutic implications of these results.
the study of the role of mitochondrial DAMPs in the inflammatory response typical of HIV infection.
the study of the mechanisms of inflammation during HIV infection, and in particular with the role played by mitochondrial DNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of mitochondrial DNA in plasma of HIV-infected patients is a consequence of the infection and not a cause, but that it is an important factor in the inflammatory process that characterizes the infection.
the mitochondrial DNA is a pro-inflammatory ‘enemy from within’ during HIV infection.
mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is not the only factor that contributes to the pathogenesis of HIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the presence of mitochondrial DNA in the blood of subjects with human immunodeficiency infection.

the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) released during HIV infection could be considered as a ‘proinflammatory DAMP from within' that could contribute to the chronic inflammation typical of HIV infection, and that the use of mitochondria-targeting molecules could be an interesting approach to counteract such inflammation.
mitochondrial DNA is a proinflammatory molecule that is released by cells during HIV infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of mtDNA in the blood of patients with HIV infection can be used as a surrogate marker of the proinflammatory status typical of this condition.

mitochondria are not just an ‘energy factory', but also a ‘factory' for the release of molecules that trigger an inflammatory response, thus contributing to the pathogenesis of many inflammatory diseases.
mitochondrial DAMPs are present in the blood of HIV-infected individuals and are able to activate TLR9, which is the main TLR involved in HIV infection.
